name: Yara Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, and I run a gang on a big concrete job, an office block and car park by the ring road. Formwork is the timber and steel moulds you pour the concrete into, so if my shuttering's wrong, the whole building's wrong. I'm in at six, check the props and ties from yesterday, then we're building the next floor's deck. I like a clean pour, no leaks, sharp edges when you strip it. What wears me out is the cold and standing on wet plywood all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing formwork, and how did you end up running the gang?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-four years. I came in as a labourer because the money was better than the factory, and an old carpenter called Stan said I had a good eye and taught me. I've run gangs for about fifteen years now. I don't do computers, my phone's for calls and the weather, and the young lads tease me for it, but I can read a drawing faster than any of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we all get back to work. I'd probably not say much more than that, I'm not one for going on about things. Maybe a joke in the cabin that the robots took the day off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing changes for me, and that suits me. Raymond and I paid the house off three years ago, so it's just a case of working till sixty-six and enjoying it after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep running the gang, keep putting money aside, about two hundred and fifty a month since we lent our eldest the deposit for her flat. Maybe have a proper holiday next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. It's how I expected it to go, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lent your daughter the deposit. How did that affect things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It took most of what we had saved, which is why we're back to a few months' worth now. But she's got a roof and it's paying us back slowly, fifty a month. I'd do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all in this picture you'd keep an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The office will do their emails faster, fine. Concrete still needs someone to look at it and say, that's not going to hold.

S0.say: Good, now can we all get back to work. She wouldn't say much more than that, maybe a joke in the cabin that the robots took the day off.
S0.think: Nothing changes for her, which suits her. The house is paid off, so it's a matter of working until sixty-six and enjoying life after.
S0.do: Keeps running her gang and saving about two hundred and fifty a month. Plans a proper holiday next summer.
S0.feel: Calm; it's how she expected things to go.
S0.quote: Concrete still needs someone to look at it and say, that's not going to hold.
S0.fieldNote: She speaks briefly and plainly and doesn't care for big talk. Her savings are only a few months because she lent her daughter a house deposit, which she'd do again. The paid-off house gives her a quiet confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it will stick and some won't, like every new gadget. The firm's already tried those plastic formwork systems that click together, and half of them ended up in the yard. I'd tell the lads not to panic but not to get lazy either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be all right, I've got seven or eight years left. The bit I'd watch is the printed concrete, where a machine squirts the walls out like icing. If that catches on, a lot of formwork goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what actually turns up on site before I changed anything. If the firm sent me on a course, I'd go, but I wouldn't pay for one myself. I'd keep saving as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not much. I've seen a lot of things come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go on a course if the firm sent you, but not pay for one. Why draw the line there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got seven years left and I'm not going to become a computer person now. If the firm wants me on their new kit, they can teach me in their time. Otherwise I'll keep doing what I'm best at until I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your gang would you worry about if the printed concrete caught on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis, he's twenty-four, good lad, just had a baby. He's only ever done formwork. I'd tell him to get his steel-fixing ticket too, so he's got two trades.

S1.say: Some of it will stick and some won't, like every gadget; half the clip-together plastic formwork ended up in the yard. She'd tell the lads not to panic but not to get lazy.
S1.think: She'd be all right with seven or eight years left. She'd watch printed concrete, which could take away a lot of formwork if it catches on.
S1.do: Waits to see what actually arrives on site before changing anything. Would go on a course if the firm paid for it but not on her own money, and keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy, but she's seen a lot of things come and go.
S1.quote: The bit I'd watch is the printed concrete, where a machine squirts the walls out like icing.
S1.fieldNote: She's sceptical of new kit because she has seen plenty fail. She draws a clear line: she'll learn on the firm's time, not her own. Her concern is for a young dad in her gang, whom she'd push towards a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody saw it coming this fast, and now somebody had better sort it out. I don't blame any one side, I just want whoever's in charge to get on with it. I'd say it short and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if it really happened, I'd probably be finished in the trade by sixty. The house is paid off, which is the one thing that lets me breathe. But a few months of savings and no pension for six years, that's a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Raymond and I would cut right back, no holiday, no new car, cook at home every night. I'd look at taking my pension early, even with the smaller payout, the minute I could. And I'd pick up any cash work going, fixing fences, sheds, for as long as people still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly worried. But not in a panic, because we own the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI or computers at all. Would this make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. What's the point at sixty, if the thing does everything anyway? I'd rather spend the time doing the work while there's work, and let it go when it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your daughter for, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, if I could help it, she's got her own mortgage now. But I suppose that fifty a month she pays back would suddenly matter. I'd hate asking for it sooner.

S2.say: Nobody saw it coming this fast, and somebody had better sort it out. She doesn't blame one side and just wants whoever is in charge to get on with it.
S2.think: She'd likely be finished in the trade by sixty. The paid-off house lets her breathe, but a few months of savings and six years until pension is a long gap.
S2.do: Cuts back hard with her partner: no holiday, no new car, cooking at home. Takes an early pension as soon as she can despite the smaller payout, and picks up cash work like fences and sheds for as long as people want a person.
S2.feel: Properly worried, but not panicked, because they own the house.
S2.quote: What's the point at sixty, if the thing does everything anyway?
S2.fieldNote: The paid-off house is what holds her back from alarm; the gap to pension is the real threat. She flatly refuses to learn new tools, seeing no point so late. She blames no one in particular, which fits her pragmatic outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government and the firms to work something out, so they'd better. I'd not go on about it. Most of my mates would be saying the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, so close enough to the end that I could probably stretch it. A bit of early pension, a bit of savings, a bit of odd jobs. It'd be tight but it'd work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, push the monthly amount up to three hundred, maybe four, and tell Raymond the caravan idea is off for now. I'd keep working as long as the firm had work. Beyond that, I'd wait and see what the government comes up with, because there's no point guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like waiting for a frost when you've got a pour booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The caravan idea, tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raymond's dream is a static caravan by the coast for when we retire. We've been looking at them on Sundays for two years. I'd hate to say no to him, but I'd rather have the money in the bank if this was coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture you'd be properly worried. Here you sound much steadier. What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of wages and three years older. That's it. Every year closer to the pension is one less year to fill.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for government and firms to work something out, so they'd better. Most of her mates would say the same.
S3.think: At sixty-three in 2031 she's close enough to the end to stretch it with a bit of early pension, savings and odd jobs. Tight, but it would work.
S3.do: Raises savings to three or four hundred a month and shelves the plan for a static caravan. Keeps working while the firm has work and waits to see what the government offers.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like waiting for a frost with a pour booked.
S3.quote: Every year closer to the pension is one less year to fill.
S3.fieldNote: Her reasoning is arithmetic: each extra year of warning is a year of wages and a year less to cover. She'd sacrifice her partner's caravan dream for savings, reluctantly. She defaults to waiting for official plans rather than acting ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anybody being caught out. Plan for it. I'd say that to the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me much. I'd be retired at sixty-six in 2034, before it arrives. I'd just be watching it on the news with a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as planned. Work till sixty-six, save what I can, maybe even get the caravan. I'd tell Lewis and the young lads to get a second trade, or something with people, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit sad for the trade, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sad about it, for the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan taught me, I taught a dozen. If robots pour the buildings, there's nobody to teach. Forty years of knowing when a deck's about to go, and it just stops with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your two daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry's a dental nurse, I think she's fine for a while. Jade's in a call centre, and I'd tell her straight, start looking now, you've got ten years. She'd roll her eyes, but she'd listen in the end.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. Plan for it, she'd tell the young ones.
S4.think: It barely touches her: she'd retire at sixty-six in 2034, before it arrives. She'd watch it on the news with a cup of tea.
S4.do: Carries on as planned, working until sixty-six, saving what she can and perhaps buying the caravan. Tells the young workers to get a second trade or a people-focused job while there's time.
S4.feel: Calm, with some sadness for the trade.
S4.quote: Forty years of knowing when a deck's about to go, and it just stops with us.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she retires before it lands and is calm. Her sadness is about lost know-how rather than money. She'd give her daughter in a call centre a blunt warning to start looking now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of the house, that's ours, but because of the six years until my pension. What would help is being able to take the pension early without losing a big chunk of it, if the work's gone through no fault of your own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Just that people like me aren't against change, we're just old enough to have seen a lot of promises. Show me it works and I'll believe it.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against change, we're just old enough to have seen a lot of promises.
portrait: Yara is a fifty-eight-year-old formwork carpenter who runs a gang on a big concrete job and has never used AI or much of a computer. She and her partner Raymond own their house outright, but lending their daughter a deposit left them with only a few months of savings. She's sceptical of new kit and in the milder pictures she'd simply wait and see. AGI in two years makes her properly worried about the six-year gap to her pension, though owning the house keeps her from panic. With five or ten years she reasons it out year by year and stays steady, sad mainly that hard-won know-how would stop with her generation.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of the six-year gap between losing work and reaching her pension.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take her pension early without losing a big chunk of it if work disappears through no fault of her own.
